name: Zoe Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I work at a mid-sized supermarket on the edge of town, the one next to the bus depot. Most days I'm on the tills from eight, then after lunch they move me to the bakery counter, slicing bread and boxing up cakes. I've been there about a year and a half, so I'm still the one who has to call a supervisor when a refund gets weird. I like the regulars, like the old man who buys one croissant and tells me the football scores.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out, and what do you actually like about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My feet and the noise, honestly. The self-checkouts beep all day, and when one jams I'm the one running over while my own queue stares at me. What I like is the people, and that when I clock out it's done, I don't take it home. My partner Jonas drives buses, so we're both shift people, and we eat dinner at strange hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say told you so, a bit smug, in the staff room. Everyone's been saying robots are coming for the tills since I started, and here we'd still be. Online I'd just share some meme about tech bosses overselling things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means the same squeeze I already have. When they put in six self-checkouts last spring, my contract stayed at thirty hours but the extra shifts dried up. So nothing radical changing isn't the same as nothing changing for me, because the slow trimming of hours carries on anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep turning up and keep asking for the bakery training, because counters still need a person. I'd keep putting a hundred a month into savings like I do now, so we have about three months covered. And I'd finally go to one of the union meetings my friend Priya keeps nagging me about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, a little tired. It's like being told the weather will stay grey. Not scary, just the rent going up every year and my pay going up a bit less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the extra shifts drying up. Which bill would hurt most if they stay gone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The rent, easily. Our landlord put it up last year and we only just absorbed it because Jonas did overtime. If his overtime goes and my shifts don't come back, the first thing to go is the little trip we save for each summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And who at work would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Doreen on the next till, who's been there twenty years and can't stand the self-checkouts. Management keeps hinting she should take early retirement, and she can't afford it. If anyone gets nudged out in a quiet year, it's her, not the shiny new machines.

say: I'd tell the staff room **told you so**, because the till robots never really arrived.
I'd share a joke online about **tech bosses** overselling their gadgets.
think: Privately, I see the **self-checkouts** already trimming my extra shifts.
A **slow squeeze** on hours and rent carries on, even if AI fizzles.
do: Ask again for **bakery training**, since a counter still needs a person.
Keep saving **a hundred a month** toward about three months of cover.
Go to the **union meeting** my friend Priya keeps asking me to join.
feel: Mostly **fine** but **tired**, like a forecast that says grey for years.
S0.quote: Nothing radical changing isn't the same as nothing changing for me, because the slow trimming of hours carries on anyway.
fieldNote: Zoe separates **hype** from her real worry, which is shift hours already lost to self-checkouts.
Her **rent** depends on her partner's overtime, so the household is tighter than her savings suggest.
She leans on **union** friends but hasn't yet acted on it herself.

steps.text: Ask the manager again for bakery counter training
Keep a hundred a month going into the savings account
Attend the next shop workers' union meeting with Priya

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we're next, just slower, and that's no reason to relax. To friends I'd say this is exactly why shops need proper unions, so the savings from all this tech don't just go to shareholders. I'd probably post something angry about it, then delete it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the thinking stuff is already creeping in. The rota is made by an app now, and the ordering for the bakery is done by a system that guesses how many loaves we'll sell. The tills aren't thinking work, but if the app decides fewer people are needed on Tuesdays, it's my Tuesday that goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the union properly this month, not just turn up once. I'd learn the ordering system so I'm the person who fixes it when it guesses wrong, because that's a skill they'll still need. And I'd look at a part-time course in something like care work, just to have a plan B.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, then a bit angry. I don't hate the technology. I hate the idea that the app saves them money and nobody asks the people on the floor how to share it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the app could take your Tuesday. Has that already happened to anyone you know?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, my friend Priya on the night shift. The app cut her from four nights to three in the summer, and when she asked why, the manager just said the system shows lower footfall. Nobody could explain it, and nobody could argue with it either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a new starter on the tills in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a new starter to learn the back-office systems, not just the scanner. The person who understands why the bread order is wrong is harder to cut than the person who just bags it. I wish someone had told me that when I started.

say: I'd tell colleagues **shop work** is next, just slower, so nobody should relax.
I'd argue the savings from new tech need sharing through **proper unions**.
think: The **rota app** and bakery ordering system already decide how many of us work.
If software decides Tuesdays are quiet, my **Tuesday shift** is the one that disappears.
do: Join the **union** properly this month and go to every meeting.
Learn the **ordering system** so I'm the one who fixes its mistakes.
Look into a **part-time course** in care work as a plan B.
feel: **Uneasy** first, then **angry** that nobody asks floor staff how to share the gains.
S1.quote: The tills aren't thinking work, but if the app decides fewer people are needed on Tuesdays, it's my Tuesday that goes.
fieldNote: Zoe sees AI arriving through **scheduling and ordering** software rather than the tills themselves.
Her anger is aimed at **shareholders**, not the technology, which fits her progressive outlook.
She's steady rather than eager: she'd learn a **proven system** at work before betting on a course.

steps.text: Sign up as a full union member this month
Learn the bakery ordering system and how to correct it
Look up evening care work courses at the college

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say out loud that this is a political choice, not the weather. If they can build a machine that does everything, they can afford to look after the people it replaces. I'd be at the protest, I think, with a sign I'd probably spell wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm scared for both of us. The thinking AI in 2028 doesn't take my till straight away, but it takes the office people and the rota and the ordering. Then around 2031 the robots come for the hands-on part, and that's my whole job, and probably Jonas's bus too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away I'd stop spending on anything extra and push our savings from three months to six. I'd start the care work course straight away instead of thinking about it, because looking after people seems like the last thing anyone wants a robot doing. And I'd keep going to the union, because one person asking for help gets nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, a bit. Three years sounds like a long time until you count it in rent payments. I'd be thirty-two with no trade and no degree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and your partner Jonas actually talk about that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd talk about whether we can still try for a flat of our own, and I think we'd agree to stop looking. Jonas would say he'll be fine, because buses need someone to deal with drunk passengers. I'd say, Jonas, they'll send a security robot for that too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said care work. Why that and not something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've watched what happens when my nan's carer comes round. Half of the job is lifting and washing, but the other half is just sitting with my nan and noticing she's not eating. I think people will pay for a human there longer than anywhere else, but honestly I don't know.

say: I'd say mass job loss is a **political choice**, not something that just happens.
I'd turn up to the **protest** and argue owners must support replaced workers.
think: Thinking AI takes the **office and rota** first; robots take my till around **2031**.
My partner's **bus job** is hands-on too, so both our incomes face the robots.
do: Cut **all extras** right away and push savings from three to **six months**.
Start the **care work course** immediately instead of just thinking about it.
Keep going to **union meetings**, because nobody gets help asking alone.
feel: A bit **sick**, because three years shrinks once you count it in **rent payments**.
S2.quote: Three years sounds like a long time until you count it in rent payments. I'd be thirty-two with no trade and no degree.
fieldNote: The **three-year robot gap** is real for Zoe, but she counts it in rent, not relief.
Both household earners are in **hands-on jobs**, which turns her worry into alarm.
She picks **care work** because she believes people won't want robots there, a hope rather than a plan.

steps.text: Cancel the summer trip and all takeaway nights
Build savings from three months up to six months
Enrol in the evening care work course this year
March with the union for support for replaced workers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have a few years, so let's use them, and I'd push the union to get retraining paid for by the companies now, not later. With friends I'd be less doom and more planning. I'd still post about it, but more like here's what we should demand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it gives me a real shot. I'd be thirty-five by then, and I'd have some years' experience. Robots coming around 2034 means I could have a care qualification by then. It's still fast, but fast with a ladder, not fast with a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the care course next autumn while still on the tills, maybe two evenings a week. I'd keep saving the hundred a month and try to add fifty. And I'd probably pick up a weekend shift in a care home once I'm qualified, to test whether I can actually do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous but less sick than the last one. Like knowing an exam is coming and you've got time to revise if you stop scrolling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the care work turns out not to suit you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I've lost some evenings and learned something about myself. My mum did care work for years and came home with a bad back, so I'm not romantic about it. But I'd rather try it at thirty than be pushed into it at thirty-five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay at the supermarket until the robots actually arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, until the day they hand me a letter. The supermarket pays the rent while I study, and the discount on food matters more than people think. I'm not going to quit a steady job to prove a point to a robot that doesn't exist yet.

say: I'd tell friends to **use the years** and push for company-paid **retraining** now.
I'd post about **what to demand**, instead of just doom.
think: Robots around **2034** means I could have a **care qualification** and experience by then.
It's still fast, but there's **a ladder** instead of a cliff.
do: Start the **care course** next autumn, two evenings a week, while keeping the tills.
Raise savings from a hundred to **a hundred and fifty** a month.
Try a **weekend shift** in a care home once qualified.
feel: **Nervous** but calmer, like an exam with **time to revise**.
S3.quote: Robots coming around 2034 means I could have a care qualification by then. It's still fast, but fast with a ladder, not fast with a cliff.
fieldNote: Five years turns Zoe's fear into a **timeline**, and she plans the course around her shifts.
Her mother's **bad back** from care work keeps her realistic about the switch.
She still expects her **till job** to go, so the mood stays anxious despite the plan.

steps.text: Start a two-evening care course next autumn
Raise monthly savings to a hundred and fifty
Push the union to demand company-paid retraining

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is enough time if governments actually do something with it, and I'd keep saying that until they do. At work I'd say don't panic, but don't nap either. Online I'd share stuff about free college courses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, the till job probably lasts until the late 2030s, so I'd be around forty when robots do the shop floor. That's long enough to change careers properly, not in a rush. What worries me is people like my colleague Ray, who's sixty and won't retrain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working the tills and the bakery for now and do the care course at a normal pace over two years. I'd keep saving, and maybe Jonas and I would actually try for a flat after all. And I'd still go to union meetings, because the help for older workers has to be fought for early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. It feels like something I can plan around rather than something that happens to me. I'd still think about it, though, every time a new machine gets wheeled into the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned your colleague Ray. What happens to him in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ray will try to hang on until his pension, and with ten years he might just make it. But if they start cutting staff in the early 2030s, he's exactly who they'll offer a deal to. I'd want the union to make sure that deal is decent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might try for the flat. Isn't that risky?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, but waiting forever is risky too. If I have a care job by 2030, I'd feel okay signing a mortgage. If I don't, we keep renting and I don't beat myself up about it.

say: I'd say **a decade** is enough if governments actually use it.
I'd tell colleagues not to panic and share links to **free college** courses.
think: My till job likely lasts to the **late 2030s**, when I'd be about forty.
I worry more for **older colleagues** like Ray, who won't retrain at sixty.
do: Keep working tills and bakery while doing the care course over **two years**.
Keep saving and consider **a flat** with Jonas if a care job lands.
Stay in the **union** to fight early for older workers' help.
feel: **Calmer**, but a new machine in the shop still **sets me thinking**.
S4.quote: If I have a care job by 2030, I'd feel okay signing a mortgage. If I don't, we keep renting and I don't beat myself up about it.
fieldNote: With **ten years**, Zoe's worry shifts from herself to older colleagues like Ray.
She'd even revisit **buying a flat**, tied to landing a care job first.
Her own income feels safe for **several years**, so the mood eases to uneasy.

steps.text: Keep working tills and bakery at the same branch
Finish a care qualification over two years
Look at buying a flat with Jonas once in care work
Campaign in the union for older workers' retraining

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no question, because both me and Jonas do hands-on work and we'd have about three years. What would help is retraining I don't have to pay for, at times that fit shift work, and some kind of income support while I'm training. Not a handout, just a bridge.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the customers. Some of the old regulars come in partly to talk to someone. A robot can scan a tin of soup, but I'm not sure anyone's thought about who those people will talk to.

headlineQuote: A robot can scan a tin of soup, but I'm not sure anyone's thought about who those people will talk to.
portrait: Zoe is **27**, a junior cashier and bakery counter assistant at a supermarket by the **bus depot**.
She lives with her partner Jonas, a **bus driver**, and has about **three months** saved.
She blames **shareholders**, not machines, and slowly moves from union talk to union membership.
Her mood tracks the **robot timeline**: worst at 2028, steadying as the warning time grows.
Her plan B is **care work**, chosen with open eyes after her mother's bad back.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because both her job and Jonas's are **hands-on** with about three years' warning.
whatWouldHelp: **Free retraining** at times that fit shift work.
**Income support** while training, which she calls a bridge, not a handout.
